## Overview

The SHAP layer works with a fitted `uniml_result` or directly with trained
mlr3 learners. It returns both standardized model input and optional raw
feature values, so the same explanation can be plotted on the scale used by
the model or on a more interpretable display scale.

This vignette assumes that `kernelshap` and `shapviz` are installed, and that
`result` was produced by `run_workflow()`. Optional native SHAP paths for
XGBoost and LightGBM require the corresponding learner packages.

## Fit a workflow

```{r fit-workflow}
library(uniml)

data <- read.csv(
  system.file("extdata", "uniml-example.csv", package = "uniml")
)
data$outcome <- factor(data$outcome, levels = c("no", "yes"))

spec <- uniml_spec(
  task_type = "binary",
  outcome = "outcome",
  positive = "yes",
  id = "id"
)
spec <- set_preprocess(
  spec,
  impute = "median_mode",
  scale = "zscore",
  encode = "onehot"
)
spec <- set_feature_selection(spec, methods = "univariate")
spec <- set_learners(spec, c("lr", "cart"), tune = FALSE)
spec <- set_evaluation(spec, ci = "none", calibration = "none")

split <- make_split(
  as_uniml_data(data, spec),
  prop = c(0.6, 0.4),
  stratify = TRUE,
  seed = 123
)
result <- run_workflow(
  spec,
  train = split$train$data,
  validation = split$validation$data
)
```

## Compute SHAP values

The model sees the processed feature matrix. `explain_shap()` can use that
matrix as `data`; `raw_data` is optional and must contain the same feature
names on the display scale.

```{r explain}
shap_data <- result$preprocess$train
result <- explain_shap(
  result,
  data = shap_data,
  n_explain = 100,
  seed = 123,
  positive = "yes"
)

result$shap
result$shap$importance
```

For multiple models, use `model = "best"`, `"all"`, or a model name in the
plotting calls. A direct learner can also be explained:

```{r direct-learner}
learner <- result$models[[1]]$learner
explanation <- explain_shap(
  learner,
  data = shap_data,
  n_explain = 100,
  seed = 123,
  positive = "yes"
)
```

## Importance, beeswarm, dependence, and interaction

```{r shap-plots}
plot_shap_importance(result, model = "best")
plot_shap_beeswarm(result, model = "best")
plot_shap_dependence(result, feature = "age", model = "best")
plot_shap_interaction(result, model = "best")
```

The importance plot ranks features by mean absolute SHAP value. The beeswarm
shows the distribution and direction of individual contributions. The
dependence plot shows the relationship between a feature and its SHAP value;
supply `color_by` to inspect a possible interaction. The interaction plot uses
the SHAP interaction values produced by `shapviz::sv_interaction()`.

All four plots are also available through `plot(result, type = ...)`.

## Clinical thresholds

For a continuous feature, `extract_thresholds()` fits a smoothed SHAP curve
and reports zero crossings, optional interaction strata, and a paper-ready
summary table.

```{r thresholds}
thresholds <- extract_thresholds(
  result$shap,
  target = "age",
  interaction = "bmi",
  min_n = 20,
  min_unique = 8
)

thresholds$zero_crossings
thresholds$paper_ready
```

The threshold search is descriptive. It should be reviewed against the
biological or clinical context and validated in an independent sample before
being used as a decision rule.
